Oblivion is my favorite Elder Scrolls title, by far. Even after playing Skyrim and Morrowind (and soon Daggerfall), I still find myself preferring Oblivion over all of them. The best thing about Oblivion is it still feels like an RPG and has involved features like spell creation (something Skyrim is sorely missing), but still feels way more modernized and way less clunky than Morrowind. 

Both of those games are still good in their own right, but I really think Oblivion hit the sweet spot and got the best of both worlds. It has better combat and stealth than Morrowind, better main quest and environments than Skyrim, and better guild questlines than either of those games. In particular, the Shivering Isles expansion is fantastic. The game even has minor immersive details Skyrim removed, from weapon durability to parchment maps to spellcrafting.

The game has definitely aged (facial animations are particularly stiff), but otherwise there is little to complain about. You can also mod this game just as easily as Skyrim, which fixes most of its issues.

Don't buy the Game of the Year Edition. Buy the Game of the Year Edition Deluxe, or you will be unable to acquire the plugins not included in this edition without paying full price for the game again.

This is a very clunky and consumer-unfriendly way to handle expansions for a game, and it is set up this way on the Steam store for no apparent reason. I've played the Game of the Year Edition and enjoyed it, and I'd like to get the other official DLCs such as Battlehorn Castle and Frostcrag Spire. However, owning the Steam version of the game, I have no way to acquire those DLCs without buying the game all over again. This is bad practice.

The game is great, but the way expansions are handled on the store is something I cannot approve.

This is quite possibly the greatest game I have ever played in my entire life (WoW: TBC is the only other contender). Where to begin? 

I'll tell you a story. I remember it was 2006 and my dad was looking for a blueray player. The only options were like 800 pounds or so, or you could buy a PS3 which had just came out. So my dad opted for a PS3 and it came with a game I had never before heard of called 'Oblivion'. I being 14 years old of course wanted to play CoD 4 instead but decided to give it a shot to see how the graphics were on the new gen of consoles. I popped the disc in, game booted up and I started a new character.

 I had no clue this was an RPG game (had just gotten into WoW) and was encouraged. After completing the intro quest and liking what I'd been playing, I stepped out into Cyrodiil for the very first time and my frickin jaw dropped. I had never seen such an incredible environment in a game before and I was blown awaay by how beautiful and colourful everything I saw was. The deer running around in the forest, the serene water and the gorgeous nightsky. Amazed instantly and I knew this game was something special. Immediately I set about just running around, not caring about finding enemies to defeat or quests.. I must have explored for a good hour or so before delving into Imperial city and figuring out what was what. It took me a while but I got onto the first quest, got to Kvatch without much trouble and then I Was blown away again when I went thru the Oblivion gate. Being 14 at the time, I was a bit frightened of the Dremora and scamps in there so I actually avoided the main questline for over a year whilst completing many many other questlines first. 

Yes, it was in fact an entire year before I completed the main questline and I'm glad that I did wait before I did so because it was an incredible day (I binged for 24 hours straight, with no internet guide to keep me from stumbling). Epic battles, evil monsters and edge of your seat quests as the story unfolded. Ending with the giant dragon in Imperial City and the equally giant battle with the Oblivion monsters which ended in victory for my character (conjurer/destruction/staff type of guy). 

But before all that I completed the fighters guild, mages guild, dark brotherhood, thieves guild AND arena questlines. I experienced nearly all of the Vanilla game before the main quest, and that it how I think this game ought to be played. 

At the time, this game was so huge for me, it blew my mind in so many ways. I spent every other weekend at my dad's glued to his 42" plasma screen playing this game for hours. Questing, exploring, conquering, trying out new builds and playstyles. Every session I discovered something new in the world. It took me weeks of playtime to experience this game fully, but I definitely have done everything there is to do in this game, including making a ladder of paintbrushes to break into the Arcane University prematurely to enchant my gear with chameleon and thus become invisible. Or duping 100 steel swords randomly in the middle of the market district.. Hey, the exploits were just as fun as the game itself sometimes!

Seriously, this game defined my existence from 14-16 years old. I'm 24 now and it's still just so good. It's not AS huge as it was, but going back to all of the old towns, the old dungeons and remembering the location of EVERYTHING is priceless. I used to lose myself in this game for hours and get lost in the game itself too. The little details I can recall with alarming clarity too. Like the bandit on the long bridge just south of Imperial city. Or the layout of all the old forts and where the enemies are and how many there are and what weapons they usually spawned with. The enchanted glass helmet in the sunken ship at the very bottom of the map I happened across one day exploring. Amazing...

I could continue to ramble, but you get the point. If you haven't played this game, I highly recommend. It is better than Skyrim in every way except in graphics- but you can fix that with a few mods and then it looks just as good if not better. I have a lot of hours on Skyrim too, but far more on Oblivion. This game, it is THE game of the decade I feel and the work BSW put into it in unmatched. The attention to detail is insane and the storylines are immense. The soundtrack too, is incredible, and I'm listening to it right now with tears in my eyes writing this review and remembering that time in my life when everything was so bright and good and the only thing I had to worry about was when I was going to go to my dad's house next to get lost in Cyrodiil.

It's Oblivion. You know it already. This is one of a couple games that I've received the most enjoyment from my whole life. The amount of freedom of action absolutely floored me at the time. I love this game for that. Probably the best story lines in the franchise also the most flavorful daedric quests. Nobody will read this, but this game meant enough to me that I felt like writing a review.

I want to preface this with an admission - I played Skyrim before I played Oblivion. When I first picked it up, I was looking to see where Bethesda had come from and was looking for another similar experience. I loaded it up and was faced with characters made of plasticine, weird dialogue and a floaty combat system that actually killed me if I just ran ahead blindly. I did not like it.

A couple of years on, I came back. I think the biggest shock for me was how different it was and I expected to understand it based on Skyrim. Oblivion is not Skyrim. It's so much more. Oblivion is colourful, funny in all the right ways and the writing... the writing for the quests is phenomenal. There are many characters that you'll find yourself remembering so much further down the line, quests that just stand out as iconic and generally a much more fantastical feeling than I ever got with Skyrim. I've loved both, but give me a choice between the two and I'll gladly step into Cyrodiil for another go. 

The combat handles like you're swinging a pool noodle, but magic is where the combat in this game shines. The level of customisation and the utility of spells is phenomenal, and when you consider how easy it can be to mod this game you can fix any niggling issues you come across. 

I don't know what it is about the NPC dialogue, but even though it's comically bad it's so warming to the heart. The characters care about the world, and even if one will sit there bringing up some major threat only to be met with a complaint about mudcrabs, they all feel connected to the place they live in. I love it.

First of all, if your question is "Should I buy this game, period?", my answer is simply: Yes.
If your question is "Should I buy this game, or skyrim?" the answer's a bit more complex. I would not say either one is better, but they're two different tastes, like vanilla and chocolate.

In this case, I would say Oblivion is the vanilla. If you're looking for a straight-up, classic medieval fantasy, Oblivion might be more your thing than Skyrim, which is "themed" around the viking-style Nords. Likewise, Oblivion has the default fantasy setting of castles and forests and rolling green plains, where Skyrim is, again, Nordic themed, and focused mostly on mountains and snow.
Because of that, and some differences in art styles, Skyrim and Oblivion look very different, to the point where I would almost say that might be the deciding factor in which game is right for you. Skyrim is very much a modern game, with fairly realistic art, and that includes the recent trend of realistic games to be primarily brown and gray. Oblivion, on the other hand, is vibrant and colorful, and perhaps a bit stylized. If you are longing for a colorful first person fantasy game, Oblivion is for you (if you're looking for a sidescroller, I'd recommend Trine). If you've been wading through the Real-Is-Brown trend, the sheer vibrance of Oblivion can be a real breath of fresh air.

As for gameplay, the two games are relatively similar. I personally prefer the spellcasting setup in Oblivion over that in Skyrim - in Oblivion, you equip spells in their own slot, rather than in a hand (which could instead be holding a weapon), whereas Skyrim just treats spells like a sword that has to be put in one of your hands. Speaking of which, you cannot dual wield in this game. If you want to play a classic sword-and-shield knight, this particular difference in mechanics is more or less irrelevant, except that it's easier in Oblivion to cast the occasional healing spell.
Furthermore, Oblivion offers a much greater degree of freedom in spellcasting than Skyrim. You can create your own spells by adding effects and designating whether the spell is a projectile, area of effect, etc. Enchanting and Alchemy are slightly more complex than in Skyrim, as well. If you like playing spellcasters, I'd say Oblivion is probably a better choice than Skyrim, which has you simply pick from pre-determined spells, and has a far more limited alchemy and enchanting system.

The biggest mechanical difference is the level up system. Without a doubt, Skyrim's level up system is more user friendly and intuitive. It might be a little more friendly to those who want to play these games casually, where Oblivion requires a little more care, planning, and effort. In Skyrim, you level up your skills as you use them, and after you've increased any combination of skills by a certain amount, you can go up a character level (on the spot, even). When you do, you increase one of your three stats (yes, only three: health, mana, stamina), and pick a talent tree to put a talent point in, which gives you bonuses - with different talent slots unlocking as you raise the respective skill. In Oblivion it is completely different. For one thing, you have several stats, each tied to three skills. The number of times you level any combination of skills attached to a given stat affects how much you could POTENTIALLY increase that stat by when you level up (and if you dont' get those +5s, you will find that the game swiftly outlevels you). By the way, you only level up when you raise ten points in any combination of your class's seven major skills, and only when you sleep. Skyrim has no classes, and therefore no major skills. This makes Skyrim's character-building system a little bit more freeform, as you can, if you want, change directions as you go, if you decide you don't like a particular aspect. Oblivion allows you to create a custom class, but you're basically stuck with that choice after you finish the tutorial.
In short, Skyrim has a simpler, more intuitive, more fluid leveling dynamic, good for building your character as you go according to what feels natural, while Oblivion might be better for those who like to plan or min-max, and requires a bit more thinking ahead.

I should also mention that on certain computer systems, the music in this game may not work. It certainly doesn't work on my system, but otherwise the game runs just fine. From what I understand this is an issue with the CODECs and may be related to Windows 7.


One other thing I think is important to mention is that this game, despite being a fantasy, is surprisingly arachniphobe friendly. As someone with arachniphobia, I find it hard to deal with how ubiquitous giant spiders are in fantasy games. Skyrim's spiders are particularly horrifying. But Oblivion has no (true) spiders at all. It does have the Spider Daedra, which are essentially spider-centaurs, but I didn't find them particularly phobia-triggering. They're also very rare outside of the oblivion gates, so you won't often find yourself being jumped by one unexpectedly. If you are an arachniphobe looking for a fantasy game, I HIGHLY recommend Oblivion, especially if you're comparing it to Skyrim.

Oblivion is still surprisingly good and I’ll try using this review to highlight some important things a player might be considering about playing this game on recent times.

[h1]1)You can use mods, but you don’t have to:[/h1]
When I was planning my most recent play of Oblivion, I though it would be necessary the use of mods. I’ve delayed starting this game for a while because of this - since Oblivion is not easy to mod as Skyrim is. Truth is that I’ve started totally vanilla and stayed that way through the end of a 100h campaign and I can say that this game holds up pretty well without any mods.

The game is still beautiful, the art is incredible, the whole visual is still appealing somehow. Mechanics works pretty well and etc. I know mods can improve a lot of things but I think modding Oblivion is not a requirement to enjoy the game today.

[h1]2)You should play on first person perspective:[/h1]
That goes for every Bethesda games mostly. Third person is janky and not cool. It works for when you want to see your character and that’s it. If you want to play a third person game I suggest going for another game. Oblivion is a first person game and this is a game change thing for me.

[h1]3)Keyboard and Mouse are game changes:[/h1]
I was always a controller guy and I had a lot of fun playing Oblivion on my old PS3 back in 2010, but that was there. Playing with KM is so much better that I can’t even tell and this is something that can totally change how you feel the game. And it’s not only about using hotkeys and having a more free control of the camera movement. It’s about just everything! Even the bad menu navigation that were based on consoles works better with KM in my opinion.

[h1]4)Some builds works better than others gameplaywise:[/h1]
The best mechanics for me is sword and shield, magic and not so much playing stealthy. That tip works for Skyrim as well. Playing a stealth build works nicely in some way, however, the mechanics are a bit dated for a stealth game - and also makes exploring dungeons way too long and a bit boring in my opinion, specially compared to newer entries on stealth mechanics over the past 15 years. So, my tip for making the best of the gameplay is playing with magic plus/or weapons and shield and going wide open exposing yourself in combat.

You can actually do what you want and playing stealthy can be a lot of fun as well. It works in the end! Just consider what I am saying specially if you feel that the game is dragging. Also, because I didn’t try all the possible builds as well so I’m just saying what I feel rather than try to set some rules here. 

[h1]5)The combat feels like “Doom or Quake” and it’s awesome:[/h1]
The combat is way more fast paced than Skyrim - and that actually depends on your build as well. Playing with a no armor mage I felt I was like the doom guy shooting magic instead of a gun, and it was awesome. On another play I tried sword and shield with heavy armor and it was way slower, but even so, more arcadish than what I feel when I play Skyrim - which is slower and heavier. 

That said, for me the most important thing to note is the timing of the enemies attacks. It is way more easier to dodge compared to Skyrim. Which makes running around and dodging multiple incoming attacks more manageable in Oblivion. And sometimes I felt like playing Quake, or Doom, for real. This makes the Oblivion combat fun and kind of unique, more closer to boomers shooters I think!


[h1]6)Pure mage is pure fun:[/h1]
Playing as pure mage is unique in Oblivion due to the quantity of spells you have at your disposal. You can do just about everything with magic: you can walk over water, breath under water, become invisible, control other players and creatures, open chests, bring objects to your hand using telekinesis, create space on your inventory by increasing how much weight you can carry, detect others around using life detection, summon creatures to help you in battle, etc. Mix all that with alchemy options and I had the best experience as a mage ever in an RPG game. The fact that you have a dedicated and separated button to magic instead of equipping as a weapon helps as well since you can use enchanted weapons with magic in a more practical way. Skyrim has the dual cast benefit, which is absent here, but I think I prefer Oblivion way. 

Oblivion has a spell efficiency mechanic that benefits no armor use. My mage wears common clothes, lol. What I did to deal with the no protection problem was using shield spells and later enchanting my clothes with  stacking shield spells as well. You can be a truly overpowered beast playing as pure mage in Oblivion and it’s so much fun since you’ll use magic for everything, all the time.

[h1]7)Sword and shield play:[/h1]
Later I did a play with a second character using a traditional sword and shield approach, but trying a custom class that included alchemy and restoration spells. The heavy armor makes the combat slower and you need to study the timing on investing attacks and raising the shields way more. It takes more attention and makes the game way harder. I think the sword fighting of Oblivion and Skyrim are still very good for a first person melee combat. It holds up pretty well and it is a different game than playing with a pure mage. 

[h1]8)The dialogs are better than I was expecting:[/h1]
There is tons of Oblivion memes on the internet regarding the fun dialog and AI. Bethesda tried what they’ve called ‘radiant AI’ for the time and it was a bit of marketing and a bit of a flaw because of not reaching the level of promising and ambitious it was intended. However, Oblivion is not a dumb game. It’s the opposite actually, since quests and story lines tend to have better explanations than what they did in Skyrim, for example. In Skyrim characters tend to be more direct to the point and this is a bit rough sometimes in my opinion. Oblivion has pretty decent lines and explanations and can be really engaging even on some small quests. That was something I wasn’t expecting so it was a nice surprise.    

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Oblivion is still a pretty decent game that can be surprisingly good even on vanilla. Gameplay is up to date, visuals can be surprisingly beautiful sometimes, the text is decent, and exploration is rewarding. Highly recommended for anyone, because I’ve never felt as I was playing an old game, for real.

Despite its age and well-known awkward NPCs, I can say that The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a lot more fun compared to it's successor, Skyrim. The quests are more fun and interesting compared to Skyrim's numerous fetch quests. The world is also more colorful, compared to Skyrim's beautiful but dreary world. The gameplay of both games are very similar, and if you've played one you won't have trouble playing and enjoying the other. In here you play as Hero of Kvatch, a person trusted with protecting the Emperor's son and stopping the Oblivion crisis.

There are also 5 factions, each with their own questlines. They are the Fighters Guild, Mages Guild, Thieves Guild, Dark Brotherhood, and Arena. You can join each of these factions without cancelling out the other. Each of them has a quite long, unique questline. Arena is an exception, since the quest is basically just defeating enemies in the Arena. They do not affect the main story, so feel free to start them anytime.

The Game of the Year Edition Deluxe includes all DLCs, but most of them only gives you items such as houses, spellbooks, and horse armor. The only ones with extra story content are Mehrunes' Razor, Knights of the Nine, and Shivering Isles. Mehrunes' Razor is a single mission DLC that's basically just one long dungeon, with the Daedric weapon at the end. 

Knights of the Nine is another DLC that adds a joinable faction, with the length of one faction questline, but a bit shorter. I recommend doing KotN in one go, as some of the quests requires you to have 0 infamy, so don't do "evil" quests or you have to do the pilgrimage again to clear your infamy. Shivering Isles is a pretty long DLC that takes place in a whole new area, the realm of Sheogorath the Mad God. There are plenty of unique items and new enemies in this DLC. Sadly, SI is the only long DLC in Oblivion.

My only problem with Oblivion is the voice actors, or lack thereof. Despite having big names like Patrick Stewart and Sean Bean, most NPCs only have two voice actors for one race, one male and one female. While this is not a problem with generic NPCs, it does make many important characters forgettable because they sound the same. Other than that, Oblivion is a very good RPG, and if you like Skyrim you should buy this one.

If you're new to this title:
Oblivion isn't a game that you play. Oblivion is a game that you conquer.
Yes, the graphics and mechanics haven't aged well. Yes, the dialogue is often hilariously unhinged. And yes, the game is ripe with bugs and quest breaking sequences that induce a paranoid amount of saving. But its' defects can also be broken in your favor. THAT realization is when the game grips you:
What can you get away with? What cheese tactics, what exploits, or what innocuous and obscure thing (like picking up and dropping a paintbrush from your inventory... this is not a joke) can you leverage to your adventure— and how far can you leverage it? And there's so much to be adventured: every nook and cranny or every dungeon, achieve and ace every quest, grind every attribute and skill to max, collect every unique item, and then, after a 100+ hours... lament that it's over.

Which brings us to those who are returning to this title:
You know as well as I that this game has near to no replay value. Everything Oblivion has to offer can be experienced in a single playthrough, and the narrative has little to no variation (nor any substantial dialogue or narrative choices for those hopping for more RP in their RPG like the CRPGs that predated it).

It can be a hell of a ride, but with a story you can only fully revel in once, as a fresh player.
Otherwise you're only left to recall the insatiable desire to see and do everything until the memory of your previous experience is restored, which quickly dulls the experience.
However, on a personal note, I will add: that one thing I recalled was that this was one of the few games that truly made me feel as though I were fighting an endless army of demons; running, jumping, and cutting through one Oblivion gate after another...

Oblivion, the game from the Elder Scrolls series that is often criticized these days. You will hear a lot of people say, "Take either Morrowind (Elder Scrolls III) or Skyrim (Elder Scrolls V), this one is not worth the trouble."

 It is true that Morrowind is undoubtedly the most successful when it comes to the role-playing aspect, character customization, a very "connected" world where your actions influence the many factions, a huge lifespan, an unusual and very immersive world, and a feeling of unparalleled character progression.

 It is true that Skyrim has the most advanced graphics, very cinematic, very beautiful, and a more dynamic gameplay than its grandpa Morrowind, with a very lively world where you will find little surprises and astonishment all over the game map, whether it is a sacked merchant's cart, a giant monster corpse, references to other games or folklore ....

Well Oblivion, it's just the middle ground between these two. This is the Elder Scrolls whith the best balance between the role-playing aspect, character creation, progression, quests, addicting scenario and the visual aspect and playability, with graphics nicer than those of Morrowind, a world more active and lively (the NPCs have a schedule, talk to each other and do not stay stuck in the same place indefinitely as in Morrowind, not to mention the FULL dubbing of all the NPCs in the game, of all the lines of dialogue!) .

Oblivion is the middle in the Elder Scrolls series. If you are looking for some old school RPG you won't be disappointed, if you are looking for an action game you will get that too. Oblivion, it is also a very classic environment. Where his predecessor proposed a twisted world, with strange monsters, giant mushrooms, houses built in shells and where his successor offers a Viking, Nordic universe, CONAN THE BARBARIAN and in that genre ... Oblivion offers Europe in the Middle Ages, with a fantastic appearance. Nothing more, classic and déjà vu, but classic well mastered, while adding its own touch. You will get lost in the oak forests of the west of the country, or in the immense golden plains of the coastal region or in the stinking marshes of Blackwood.

Oblivion is choosing not to choose from the Elder Scrolls series, and being sure you won't be disappointed.

And it is without mentioning the DLC, which are excellent, in particular Shivering Isles which is undoubtedly one of the best expansions out of all the Elder Scrolls to date.

I was introduced to the Elder Scrolls series about 20 years ago when Morrowind came out. I was kinda young and didn't really get that far. But when Oblivion came out, I was absolutely addicted! I had this game on Xbox 360 originally and must have put in over a thousand hours into it. Then, when I switched to PC; I got it on disc version. Finally, I ended up getting it on Steam too. 

What can be said about this title for those who love Skyrim, but have never played Oblivion? The transition might be hard for you... The graphics are vastly outdated now (Heck, even Skyrim is), the combat system is very simplistic. The NPCs are absolutely ridiculous and can't be taken seriously... 

That being said... Oblivion is vastly superior to Skyrim in every other way. Let's take the mages guild as an example. In Skyrim, you join up with the college with next to no difficulty at all. Your first assignment is to go on a little field trip. On that first assignment, you uncover something that leads you on a small-ish journey. By the end of that journey, you become the Archmage for some reason... That's it. You're done... In Oblivion, you must travel across the entire province of Cyrodiil. You must visit every single chapter of the Mages guild, where you learn new spells, are imparted with wisdom and knowledge of all things magical and collect recommendations from all the chapter heads. Once you have been recommended by every single chapter, you are permitted to join the University. You are now an Apprentice! Your first task is to go collect wood and such to construct your first staff. You also now have access to creating your own spells (Amazing system!). Hooray, all those hours of travelling the province for those recommendations has paid off! But you're just an Apprentice... The journey is just beginning. You slowly carry out tasks for your master and rise the ranks, 1 by 1. You become more powerful and you get closer and closer to the top of that career ladder. Eventually, a big villain is introduced who could have easily been a villain of an entire game. You end up vanquishing him and saving the Mages Guild and rise to the esteemed rank of Archmage after proving yourself over time and time again. 

That is the difference between Skyrim and Oblivion. This same scenario is repeated for every single faction! I can't express how much I resented Skyrim for how crap the guild factions were... 

Anyway, the game is ridiculously cheap so if you can get past the outdated graphics, simplistic game mechanics and goofy NPCs... You'll find a gem in Oblivion!

While people complain that the Elder Scroll games can be quite bland and you play an expressionless psychopath mass murdering your way to the top of society, Oblivion is a sterling example of one of my favourite things about PC gaming - mods. Oblivion really captures the DIY aspect of PC gaming I love in a shiny giant studio package, allowing me to change almost anything i don't like about vanilla.  Unlike console people, to merely review and make judgements based on vanilla is to miss the beauty of PC gaming.  It's that kind of community that keeps an aging game fresh interesting and addictive.

As far as the extras in the GOTY go, whether you care about player houses shapes much of  the DLC, Mehrune's Razor quest is a large dungeon, nothing mind blowing if you play with Lost Spires mod, but some very shiny loot.  The Knights of the Nine was a fairly straight-forward quest, would call it a good DLC rather than an expansion pack as such.  However although you have to seriously stab someone at the end, at least some of the quests have variety in what you have to do a bit.  

However Shivering Isles makes this edition worth your money imo.  It adds some much needed oddness to the game, the kind of thing where you pause to think 'wtf is that?' as some creature shuffles or leaps towards you.  Without getting into the whole 'which elder scrolls is best', one thing i felt was Oblivion and Skyrim settled with standard pseudo-medieval europe fantasy world, whereas Morrowind felt quite alien, but with it's own culture to be read about and discovered.  Shivering Isles brings that to Oblivion.  The books are a delight, and it's nice to experience a daedric realm aside from the Deadlands (which while fun, never felt like a place people lived).  All in all and bearing in mind what i said about the still quite vital mod community, I totally recommend you buy this game.

I ended up having to go through 3 different managers as I progressively ran into various incompatibilities.
- Oblivion Mod Manager (OMM) can't handle scripted installs and has a very painful manual mod creation process from zip files as opposed to simple import.
- TES Mod Manager is the successor of OMM that can handle scripts, but has performance issues and freezes a lot (took 5 minutes to add each mod, game ended up crashing on launch).
- Nexus Mod Manager (NMM) is too new and a lot of older mods don't work with it.
- Vortex has the same issue as NMM.
- Wrye Bash seems supported by quite a few mods, but is not very user friendly. I didn't try it as MO2 did the job.

Easily one of the best TES titles

The music in this game is iconic, the best of the series, easily.
Graphics are old. What did you expect? But there are always mods to fix the faces.. the landscape, however, is beautifull, and you can enhance that with mods too!

The combat is similar to skyrim, but faster.. In fact this was the first TES title that did away with the whole dice roll system.. which is a good or bad thing, depending on where you’re coming from.

This was the last TES title with a good magic system. In every TES except Skyrim, you could create custom spells and enchantments, which makes the magic system quite limitless. You can create any kind of spell you can imagine, with any effects in the game. Though you have to reach a certain point in the Mage’s Guild Questline before you get access to the spellmaking and enchanting altars..

Which reminds me: faction questlines!

I cant think of a single faction with a bad questline... every one of them has a very well written story and had twists and turns that you wont see coming... the Dark Brotherhood questline is famous!

Stealth is weird, and i dont have much experience with it... plenty of spells, enchantments and effects to help you be mire stealthy though..

Perks are unlocked automatically when you level up certain skills. The perks are, unfortunately, quite unoriginal and generic, which is a shame...

Leveling can be weird... every time you level up, you increse 3 attributes.. how many points you get depends on how much you’ve used those attributes.
Use magic a lot, and you’ll get a lot of points in intelligence and willpower. Fight a lot, you’ll increase strength and endurence. Sneak and use archery a lot, your agility’ll go up etc. etc.

This system is bad and can result in a really, really bad and innefective build quite quickly... which sucks.. thankfully there’s...

Mods. There’s less mods than skyrim, and they vary in quality by a wide margin, but theres a lot of good ones. The game can quickly become unstable though, so be ready for that...

DLCs and Expensions. This game literally invented DLCS. Horse armor much? But you can read about that everywhere else...
This game has 2 major expansion packs and a bunch of smaller DLCS. The expension packs are good, especially Shivering Isle. Knights of the Nine is decent enough.. The DLCs range from player homes to horse armor and spell tomes.. They all come in the GOTY edition though so you dont have to worry about those...

Finally, the Oblivion Gates. Oblivion Gates are a major part of the main questline, and they'll end up everywhere.. You cant swing a dead cat in the wild without hitting one oblivion gate.

They're... well, they're decent, but repetitive. Basically the way they work is you got a big tower in the middle, you gotta climb it to the top, take the big laser gem and get booted out. Thats it. But between the gate and the gem, you get a bunch of enemies, obstacles, traps, puzzles etc. 
Oblivion gates range from short and simple to ridiculously maze-y and annoying. Every time i enter that one cave gate, i just tcl my way to the tower because feck that sh*t...
They're a good source of loot, i guess, and the sigil stones are a good way to get your gear enchanted, though the enchantments are random..

Overall, Oblivion is a gem of a game. Its my favourite TES title (though Morrowind is a very close second), and i always feel at home whenever i launch Oblivion and hear the epic main menu theme song...

The first time I played Oblivion, I hated it. I thought it had the worst character models of all time, and the combat took too long and felt unnecessarily difficult, I immediately developed the opinion that Skyrim was the best game in every regard. That was probably one of the biggest mistakes I've ever made concerning a video game. The thing about oblivion that makes it the polar opposite of Skyrim is that, the more you play Oblivion, the better it gets. Meanwhile Skyrim is magical at first, and then progressively gets way too easy and tedious. So heres why you need to play Oblivion in 2016:
1) The combat
As mentioned antecedently, Oblivion combat system is fucking retarded at first, but then, very similarly to Morrowind, you feel yourself getting progressively more powerful. You start as someone less dangerous than a native american toddler with cerebral palsy, but turn into one of the most epic warriors on the face of Tamriel. It also requires more skill, you need to strafe and blocking actually consistently makes a difference in who falls first in an engagement. Although there are no fancy decapitation animations, it still rewards more of a sense of completion, since you know that you have to be powerful to slay this person or creature.
2) The Story
Oblivions many storylines, particulary the Dark Brotherhoods, blow skyrim out of the water. The characters have so much more depth than, "I came from X and I'm gonna hostile to you now but after one fucking quest I'm gonna worship the ground you walk on" They will start to like you more after every few assassinations, depending on how well you perform them, and when its done, you wont just be their favorite warrior, you will be their leader. Same with the main quest, rather than just running around dungeon to dungeon, killing the draugr "boss" at the end. There are many different types of quests within the main storyline, and honestly it feels like a complete movie at a certain point.
3) The quests
You know whats better than having to go into a tunnel fight the draugr minions, fix a puzzle with the directions right in front of you, and have it be the same puzzle every time? EVERYTHING is the answer to that. Oblivion has such a vast arsenal of different variations of quests that it can throw at you, poisoning someones food, chasing a unicorn, etc
4) The world
The final point I'm going to rant about is that the world of Oblivion is more interesting than Skyrims in almost every regard. The people have their own conversations, and the game somehow manages to give personality to all of the random conversations as well. For example, when a nord and an imperial had a conversation, the imperial said, "those nords sure are hostile" and he immediately said goodbye. That sort of discomfort in the face of racism adds so much personality and says alot about the world itself, and the bigotry is hurled in every direction from every direction. It also, despite a weaker engine, still looks prettier, due to its bright colors rather than white and brown.

[h1] Don't skip this assuming it's inferior to Skyrim; in many ways, it's the better game [/h1]
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is the game that set the template for modern Bethesda games (both the Elder Scrolls and Fallout series), and (because the formula was so successful) modern open world games in general.  Like any modern open world game, you always have access to an in-game map with quest markers shown clearly all over the place; you will never get lost.

In some games, this doesn't work well and you feel like you're just following the arrow from one objective to the next.  Oblivion does the same thing, but the quests are varied and interesting enough that it somehow works.  It helps that there are actually very few of the typical "collect five rat tails" kind of quests you find in lesser games.

Oblivion has a very satisfying main quest, but it's also very enjoyable to just roam around exploring and setting your own goals.  As you wander around town, you'll see and hear NPCs having conversations with one another; listening to these can sometimes even clue you in to optional quests.  It's a very cool touch and makes the world feel a bit more believable, even if the conversations end up becoming complete ridiculous the longer you listen to them (they are not scripted, but somewhat random).

Although I was able to complete the main quest (and lots of other content) in only 40 hours, I really only scratched the surface of what this game offers, Oblivion is truly a game you could play for hundreds of hours.  Highly recommended!

[b]Knights of the Nine[/b]
A fun little quest that begins with you seeking out a bunch of shrines while referencing a "hand-written" map. Oblivion makes some arguable improvements over Morrowind, as well as some massive steps backwards. Some of these mistakes would be fixed in Skyrim, while others will be ignored or worsened in some sense. As a full experience, Oblivion is a big open, sometimes annoying, technically and gameplay wise, but still mostly enjoyable overall. However, unlike Morrowind, where if you looked past the graphics now you could likely get immersed, Oblivion has numerous barriers preventing it from matching Morrowind.

Compared to Skyrim, the combat feels somewhat choppier. It is faster at some points, but it manages to feel a lot more simplistic. I definitely prefer non-magic combat over Morrowind's dice roll simulation however, as combat finally feels responsive. Magic crafting also returns from Morrowind, and still feels very powerful at higher levels. However, I actually, for whatever reason, prefer magic in Morrowind to Oblivion. Learning a school of magic however, unlike Skyrim, is still worth doing regardless of playstyle due to the ability to cast regardless of whether both hands are occupied or not. Oblivion is, combat wise, the halfway point between Morrowind's more traditional style and Skyrim's faster combat, so benefits and pros of both apply here. I don't actually mind it, as like I said, magic feels superior to Skyrim, while in most other areas, combat feels more responsive than Morrowind.

Location-wise and graphically, Oblivion is very green and bright. It has a better colour pallet than non-modded Skyrim, and there are definitely graphical improvements over its prequels. However, the location itself is generic. It's all greens and old elven architecture and medieval towns, rather than the alien lands of Vvardenfell's plains or Skyrim's cold mountain ranges. My main problem with Bethesda worlds has always been the very small population, and the Imperial City, although more populated than anything in Skyrim, still feels empty, and the NPC's all have very funny looking faces. Character models in Bethesda games always feel like the lack, and Oblivion is a prime example here. What feels like a let-down is that the beast races no longer have unique animations either for movement. This is more an immersion thing, and animations never affect your gameplay experience, but if you had played Morrowind before Oblivion, you'll likely notice it.

The soundtrack is quiet and peaceful. The scores are always nice in Elder Scrolls games, and although I don't have anything in this game I prefer over Morrowind (which Bethesda seemed to like as they were re-using the compositions even before the Dragonborn DLC in Skyrim), the music all fits and helps build on the games atmosphere, which is all you need a soundtrack to do.

The guild quests in Oblivion are some of the best in the series. Although the main quest becomes a bit of a drag, the Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood in particular have some of Bethesda's best quests and plotlines to them. Highlights include the Gray Fox and his final heist, and The Dark Brotherhood as a whole. There aren't any quests in Skyrim that compete with the quests here. The Fighter's Guild also has a few interesting ones and the Mages Guild suffers from the same problem that the College of Winterhold suffers from in that you can be hopeless with advanced magic and become the archmage in a few days of joining. The Arena is a massive missed opportunity, as fights never feel that big and the questline can be dusted off in about 30 minutes, which is massively disappointing. Guilds are definitely stripped back from Morrowind, due to the removal of skill barriers between the low and high ranks. Although this means that the player will be able to see everything, it means that unless you force yourself to roleplay, you can see everything on a single character. This is something even Skyrim dodged with its Civil War questline. This becomes even more self-defeating if you originally played it on the XBOX 360, and you were allowed to pick up every achievement on a single character.

The Shivering Isles expansion included is brilliant. You have to play it more than once to see everything, and although a bit short, gives a far more varied world than Cyrodiil to explore, and Sheogorath and the residents of the isles have fun, over-exaggerated personalities that fit perfectly with the theme of madness and misery the expansion is going for.

Oblivion is a big fun stupid RPG. The best ideas of Skyrim seemed to appear here, albeit somewhat under-developed, and although not as focused as Morrowind, it still maintained the RPG gameplay that Bethesda seems glad to phase out more and more as they release more games themselves. Worth a buy, and with mods, just like all the other popular Bethesda games, if it doesn't crash, you can go on and on, possibly even fixing your own personal problems with the game.
This is one of those games where it's a fun game, and when you play it you think to yourself "this is a fun time".

Boy, here we are, one of the more controversial TES games for no real reason other than two different crowds clashing each other. One coming from Morrowind, and one coming from Skyrim, they tend to leave in their wake a simple verdict of calling Oblivion bad for reasons oft subjective. Maybe it's a way to maintain the armistice between them by agreeing that at least this thing is worse than whatever they're fighting for.

They never look at Oblivion on its own.

And they really should.

The good:

This is and Elder Scrolls game, so it's expected to get a sandboxy world with lots of things to do - and Oblivion delivers exactly that. Cyrodiil is a big swath of green that's dotted with locations to uncover and aggressive fauna to beat the snot out of. You'll definitely find something to entertain yourself with.
Story/Quests. This game lacks the sheer density and cohesion of Morrowind, but it's still second best in the series when it comes to the writing in it. The only major retcon(Cyrodiil being temperate eastern european plain instead of dense jungle) isn't going to ruin anything and the quests in this game make sure you don't get distracted by the tiny details like it. Especially the Dark Brotherhood. Trust me, you want to do that questline, it's bloody amazing.
DLCs. I'm separating them from the story since KOTN and Isles give you things that are separate enough to not intervene but are so good it's worth mentioning. 
KOTN takes you on a nice adventure that involves an elf-slaying terminator called Pelinal Whitestrake that did absolutely nothing wrong. Worth noting is that it brings some dank lore and has interesting puzzles as well as a very nice woah-moment near the end that involves game's physics.
Shivering Isles could easily be a game of its own, but it isn't, but it really should've been. You take a tour of the local Wonderland that belongs to the god of insanity, Sheogorath, and it's about as wild of a ride as you'd expect from the god of loonies. Involves beating this shit out of another god, torturing people for your own amusement and dealing with literal lunatics.

The bad:

Graphics. No beating around the bush, this thing's ugly as sin. The bloom is nuclear, the character models and animations are horrifying and overall image is just smeared with vaseline. Of course, all of this can be modded out, but I ain't reviewing mods here.

The ugly:

It's a long list if I list everything, so let's just collapse into one big subpoint.
The jank.
This game is jank incarnate. Combat is jank, horses are jank, some quests are jank, performance can be jank for no real reason.
Can this all be fixed with mods? Yes.
Am I reviewing the mods? No.
Is this a problem that can turn you away if you were to play without said mods? Absolutely, but it's a case of opinion, not fact. It didn't turn me off back in the day and it doesn't entirely turn me off now.

Verdict?
If you're willing to tolerate jank, you're getting one hell of a diamond in the rough.
With all the DLCs, some mods and willingness to just [b]deal with it[/b], this game can be polished to near perfection while still remaining its own thing and not losing its identity.
And without the mods you just get a good, if janky, game.

Reviewing Oblivion sets up a huge trap for people involved. Time and time again, Oblivion reviewers fail to show any love to the game that totally deserves it. They much rather mention its imperfections, flaws and irregularities, instead of commending the game for what it does admittedly well. They tend to downplay and understate all the good, while emphasize and accentuate all the bad and unfulfilled. 

To me, Oblivion made undeniable steps in the right direction in terms of its gameplay and gameplay systems: for how ever ambitious and at first glance elaborate Morrowind systems seemed to be, they failed to work: from spammy and unsatisfying melee, to clunky magic interfacing and casting, to repetitive and way too extensive dungeons; all things combined made last 50 hours of my original Vvardenfell exploration boring, tedious and exhausting. Oblivion, on the other hand, was fairly successful in engaging me with its newer systems, giving me at least some working tools and creating at least some challenge in blade combat and offensive magic; clearing 80% of Oblivion's dungeon made me less bored and depressed comparing to Morrowind, for sure. Its greatest enemy was probably enemy sponginess on higher levels and higher difficulty, which made it impossible to balance challenge and tedium without modding enemy's health/player's damage to make it work at least somehow. Directional attacks were a welcome variety in melee, but the delay between command and attack outcome and slow animations usually made them useless: why would you even try to perform a backing-up attack if you whiff half of the time and lose a lot of fatigue and create a window for enemy attack in result? But the lesson we should carry out from this is not that these systems were bad, and old chance-based combat in theory was better, but that the systems were just underdeveloped and still could lead to a better gameplay engagement in the end.

Trimming down the set of skills was unfair to some of the interesting ones from Morrowind, but at least it made the leveling more focused, and the additional bonuses for mastering a skill were very attractive and ultimately useful. Requirements for training a skill point were ridiculously high, which is why reaching a master level in most of the desirable skills was impossible without cheating, and failed to create an illusion of different character builds being capable of mastering only few selected paths. But ultimately, for me it was still the most satisfying set of skills out of 3 modern games: imperfect, but working, no denial in that.

Infamous Oblivion quests and storylines were certainly very flawed, naively written and in desperate need of dev testing and QA. However, again, people made it too critical about the nature of the quests and their connection (or disconnection) to the lore. I could not deny that how ever obviously weak and imperfect were these quests, some of them still managed to make me feel something, make me engaged. I respect the craft when I see it, when I experience it and when I enjoy it, and I'm not willing to downplay that. Even the Dark Brotherhood, the most obvious highlight of the faction writing, nowadays gets "good, for a bar that is already set so low", which is a ridiculous understatement. Love, acknowledgement, recognition and a fair bit of critique is what it deserves, but from reviewers it was more of a disregard and indifference. This should show that over the years, the thing that Bethesda started to lack the most is quality writing and clever writers behind it, not that they totally fail to follow their own lore because the new writer is indifferent to it.

People actively discussed and questioned the game's lore, speculated on how could the missions be better if only they acted more faithfully with the lore, which is indeed a very interesting point. But they rarely invite us to take a look on a bigger picture, on how Morrowind's enormous, extensive and cryptical lore might have been the most crucial thing that actually made the game work, that gave life to its lifeless and static landscapes, gave meaning behind its sites and architecture, gave believability to NPCs written dialogue and lack of visual and graphical fidelity. The player that read the written dialogue gave it more power, more meaning than it might have actually had. The player would imagine how it would ideally sound like, which helped to immerse themselves in the world even deeper. Oblivion's seeming lack of such a focus on extensive lore made players pay more attention to the game world itself, which this time in comparison to Vvardenfell felt genuinely more dynamic and alive, but still lacking in realism and believability, failing to suspend our disbelief and giving no reason to think deeply about what we see in the world.

Oblivion's infamous voice acting, at its best, definitely enhanced the character interactions and player's immersion in the world. Imagine if every voice line got the director attention like Lucien Lachance... Sadly, everywhere else, it felt exactly like weakly directed voicing of a written dialogue, with little to no "acting" due to the sheer amount of lines and catastrophic lack of voice actors. Still, Wes Johnson, Jonathan Bryce and Michael Mack deserve huge respect from me, for their capabilities and charisma that they brought to the characters. The Oblivion voice acting remains one of the most unique artefacts of the gaming world, and should be experienced by more people in-game, not in random Youtube compilations.

OST's by maestro Jeremy Soule, probably the only consistent 10/10 thing in every modern Elder Scrolls game, are the pivotal thing in the perception of TES games, in the unique bond they create between player and the game itself. There's a reason why Harvest Dawn became synonymous with Oblivion itself, Oblivion's idiosyncrasy and quirks, Oblivion's brilliancy and yes, Oblivion's NPCs. You could talk endlessly about how Jeremy Soule's soundtracks evolved from game to game, how Bethesda finally managed to learn how to properly handle the game music, categorize between exploration, town and dungeon tracks, show at least some effort in managing flow and transitions between pieces... How Jeremy Soule took a step back from his early style of sometimes strangely, but ultimately smartly and wonderfully composed pieces of individual music, that in Morrowind resulted in an impeccable album of magnificent tracks, specializing on multiple instruments running several parallel melodic lines to create inimitable sense of harmony, soft-to-powerful dynamics, melodic and thematic meaningfulness... and adopted a more focused and eased-up approach to create music that accompanies, complements the game: different tracks for town, exploration and dungeons, music with a selected lead instrument that is supported, not interfered by other voices, music that holds it melody for longer, creating a relaxed, otherworldly and serene feel that is most associated with Oblivion's overworld scenery. 

I don't understand why almost no people analyze TES soundtracks to the extent that it deserves. Too many people listen to it, but all of them only manage to mention "nostalgia" as a factor. But the music itself is much more: it's an astounding achievement for game soundtracks, an immense source for deep feelings, a masterpiece that continues to prove Jeremy Soule as possibly the greatest auteur of the video game soundtracks.

The game deserves so much criticism, it's impossible to express all of the things in one sitting. But these days, what Oblivion deserves more than ever, is love, respect and acknowledgment for what it does well, and for what it manages to share with us. Don't be afraid to show you love for Oblivion, people.

Another flaw for me personally is the difficulty setting. Finding the perfect sweetspot varies from character to character. What i would more prefer is something along the lines of fallout 4's survival mode damage, where you and enemies both have increased killing potential. That aside, this game has characteristics that far outweigh the cons. My personal favorite being the music. This game's soundtrack, in my honest opinion, is amazing. I feel myself getting lost in the harps, flutes, and violins when wandering the various cities. Ominous music kicking in when i enter an unexplored cave. But who could forget the epic tones of the games title screen. Another great thing about this game are the secrets hidden throughout the landscape. Perhaps a bow or chest that you would have never stumbled upon in a first playthrough. Another topic i wanted to touch on is how you play this game. If you are the type of person that loves getting to the end fast and wants instant gratification, maybe this isnt your game. I think you have to be the observant type, listen to the dialogue, read the books, dont rush through every quest like you are in a hurry like so many others do. You miss out on the little nuances the game so delicately hides. You can appreciate the game on another level. These are just my thoughts on the game, the may not be true or objective, but i hope i can convince someone to experience this game the way i have. Much love and thank you for reading.

[b][u]-Quick Review-[/u][/b]
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a massive open world game developed by Bethesda and released March 20, 2006. It would take too long to list all the various quests, armor, weapons, enchantments, and magic spells you can learn/create, simply trust me when I say this game is an adventure waiting to happen.

[b][u]-Detailed breakdown review-[/u][/b]
[b]Story:[/b] This is probably one of my personal favorite parts of Elder Scrolls of Oblivion, once you get out of the starting area you can make your own story, or follow the main story, or go search for your own quest. If you wanted, you could become a villain, you could also become a hero. The choices are completely up to you.
The whole Elder Scrolls series is very rich is lore and diversity of environment, you can read in-game books and learn useful facts about the monsters you fight. Not everyone will do this, but I ended up learning what all Trolls are weak against, and I've been using it in all Elder Scrolls games since.
I won't say much more about the story, because most of the fun is in finding the quests and stories yourself, and of course forging your own tale.... however there is one additional thing to note, in the Game of the Year Edition you get the Shivering Isles Expansion, and there you meet my favorite character in the whole series.

[b]Game Play:[/b] You can control the camera to play in third person, or first person. (personally I always thought third person looked silly... the knee's bend funny, and when you jump your legs stay straight. seems like an indication of "play in first person").
You could be a necromancer and summon skeleton hoards, you could be a thief and sneak into combat, you could be a warrior and smash your enemies faces in, you can be a mage and even create your own skills, you can be a ranger and pew pew, a monk, an acrobat or any hybrid combination of what I've said and much much more.

[b]Achievements:[/b] There are no Steam Achievements in this game, you can certainly find plenty of challenges online to test your skill in the game, or simply increase the difficulty of the game.

[b]Price[/b] The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Edition is priced at $19.99, as always, I suggest you wait for a sale, but if you already know you like this style of game you won't lose money out of it, since the game is getting "old" [i]*cough cough cough*[/i] you should probably look for a good deal out of the game, it goes on sale often.

[b]Conclusion:[/b] This was the first Open world game I ever played, I absolutely loved it, and I still remember the fun I had playing the game. The stories/quests are very memorable and the game play was dynamic and very fluid. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys open world or RPG's.

Coming from Skyrim it takes a little bit of getting used to, but if you want something that bridges the gap between the simplicity of Skyrim and the complexity of Morrowind, this game is perfect for that. I actually like a lot of the features in this game more than in Skyrim. Lockpicking feels like it's a skill you can actually learn and not just random chance that you can waste perk points making less random. The voice acting is insane compared to Skyrim. So many people in that game sound so tired and unenthused. Oblivion's characters are the complete opposite. Exploration is more fun when you don't have a giant white arrow pointing you exactly where you need to go at all times. I can see why people don't love the persuasion minigame, but I kinda love having little minigames like that that I can use to gain certain characters' favor to then get different chat options out of them or even haggle for better trade prices. The level up system is also much better than in Skyrim in my opinion. First, it gives you a reason to sleep. Second, leveling up in Skyrim, especially at higher levels, sucks when you can only choose a single perk among like two dozen perk trees. In Oblivion, you can level up three "perk trees" (they're not perk trees in Oblivion but they're what turned into them in Skyrim) and each of those perks will often have several points added instead of just one. The magic systems in both Oblivion and Skyrim have their merits, but there is something I like very much about being able to have a specific spell hotkeyed that I can use at any time while having my main weapons equipped (Skyrim kinda has this with shouts, but it has a long cooldown compared to what you can do in Oblivion with magicka and a few potions). The music in both games is perfect for different reasons. There's not really much reason to compare these, one is emulating a rural nordic sound and the other is going for a bombastic imperial sound (though some of Oblivion's cave music makes me feel like Indiana Jones).
I'm not sure what my point is anymore, so let me get back to that. Oblivion is good. If you like Skyrim and you want that but with more freedom, complexity, and apparently better quests (I can attest that the earlier story quests are better imo than Skyrim's, but I'm excited to get to the later ones like the Dark Brotherhood and other faction questlines that people have been telling me about for years now), I think it's worth a shot.
Okay, enough rambling. Game good, me likely.

Oblivion, in my opinion, is the best game of all time. It gets a bad reputation among fans of other elder scrolls games, you see the argument that Morrowind is the game for patient players that can enjoy an older game, and skyrim is this big new awesome RPG, and so Oblivion is seen as some weird spot in the middle of the two. Yet I repeat, oblivion is the best game I have ever played. 
Many Morrowind players dislike Oblivion with the argument that it is less inclusive and immersive than Morrowind. But then why is Skyrim the only game on par with Morrowind? Skyrim, the game with less weapon types, the game with the worst alchemy, the game with the worst magic? Skyrim's graphics barely surpass the incredibly captured beauty of Cyrodil, and they had five years to make skyrim. They had four to make Oblivion, and your blind grandma could easily tell the difference between that and Morrowind graphically. The gameplay was also a complete overhaul from morrowind to oblivion. People talk about how Morrowind's or Skyrim's fighting systems are so much better, with Morrowind's realistic feel that you have to be good with the weapon type or you will be awful, or with skyrim's realistic feeling combat but Oblivion completely build anew the combat system of morrowind, made it insanely more realistic, and remains the only game in the series that you can have a sword, shield, and spell at the same time. 
From Morrowind to skyrim each game got easier. Morrowind is the most difficult of the three, with no quest markers on a compass, and no advice or help whatsoever. But when I went to play skyrim it was the easiest thing in the world. Anyone can take a nord with a battleaxe and beat the game. Oblivion is in the middle. Oblivion isn't like the insane difficulty of morrowind, showing how hard each quest would be were you actually to do it in real life and record the words that someone said to find a secret location. Oblivion helps you, but is not easy. The game has an easier start, but if you can remain powerful past level 30, that's when you know you're good. Skyrim is just always easy. Progress through oblivion is kind of like progress through life. The lower your level, the less you have to worry. But as you grow into the game it takes constant effort and maintenance to remain successful. In oblivion you have to have a gameplan. Will you be a thief that goes around and gets rich to make sure they have the best equipment in the game, and talks your way out of hard situations? Will you be the the brute warrior that relies on lots of stamina and power to take down less physically gifted enemies? Or will you be my personal favorite, the mage that can go about every situation in a million different ways? Sure, you can mesh these things to any degree, but the point is that if you don't go about it correctly with skills that make sense together or you use the wrong race, you won't be successful later on.
You could go on forever about the systems in place in oblivion that make it unique and amazing but Oblivion is the game that revolutionizes combat and especially graphics (Oblivion had some of the best graphics the world had ever seen, and was made on such a large scale that's almost an unimaginable feat) but sticks true to the elder scrolls mentality. Skyrim is a game to pull people into the franchise. Skyrim is the start of a new generation, a worse generation, of TES players. Oblivion is the peak in the series.

Right after its release, Oblivion divided people into many patterns. I've heard friends who felt it was not a big step above Morrowind. In other words, they were disappointed with how little was changed. They wanted more of new game design decisions, and Oblivion, following all basic guidelines of the previous games, was not such a huge leap forward that someone expected. At the same time, there were others, who felt lost and enraged with the number of obscurities in compare with their beloved TES 3. "Conspiracy of simplification", some people called new trends, shown in the Oblivion. "They trading deep, thoughtful gameplay for WOW moments!"...

It's been almost a decade since then. We saw Skyrim, Fallout 3 & 4, many other open-world RPG and wanna-be RPG titles. While it's a common thought that Oblivion was not a bad game, the main question is - Is it worth something now? If you haven't played it before, by what conditions would you like that game and will be motivated to actually play it? Simply put - should you buy it now?

In the line of Elder Scrolls games, despite common lore, every volume is quite unique. Morrowind goes with oriental motives, religious cults, and huge, comprehensive and insane magic sandbox. Skyrim is about Nords, snows, dragons and their powers, and really huge open world to explore. Really, like hundreds of hours of adventuring...

TES IV has its own focus - the Central province of Empire, being overrun with hordes of demons from the lower plane called Oblivion. The problems of central governance and very dramatic main storyline, with all adventuring and other freeride activities pushed away in favor of highly orchestrated quests. The Empire in perils, the one and only Emperor dead, along with all legal heirs... The high dosage of Pathos seems unavoidable. Is it a bad thing? No. The Oblivion still much more free-play oriented than, say, Dragon Age Origins or Witcher. And those "orchestrated" quests are not giving the feeling of moving in the narrow intestines of the scenario where you're more of the observer rather than an actual actor. Some of those quests will be memorized as perfect examples of quest-writing and performing. You know, the gold book of RPG quests, bonfires, fanfares, all that stuff...

Sure, the creators of Oblivion dropped many of the gameplay mechanics that Morrowind fans were proud of. On the other hand, we've got a world much more alive and reflecting with your actions, than it was before. All those things that were simply nailed to the one place in Morrowind, including god-like beings like Vivec - in Oblivion have not only a place to be, but the duties to perform and some logic to praise or disregard the course of current events in the game plot. Although... less static doesn't necessarily means good dynamics. It is safe to say that the world of Oblivion is not that capable of providing the player with adventures as Skyrim. Besides the main storyline and some of the fraction quests (like assassins or Daedric quest lines), some of us could even find that Oblivion is somewhat dull. On the contrary, the world of Skyrim is noticeably less colourful, so there certainly will be others, who like Oblivion More than Skyrim...

Do you know that? You should try it for yourself. Placing yourself in the sabatons of the knight-by-fortune, saving the Empire from fires of Abyss...

I remember [i]Morrowind[/i] feeling a bit overwhelming with its sheer size and scale (in a good way, of course), while [b]Oblivion[/b] takes a different approach—its richness. A short stroll through the Imperial City and you forget all about Uriel’s mission, getting swept up in countless side quests. Tasks are handed out at every corner: even a casual conversation with a passerby might spiral into a long adventure across the entire continent.

The role-playing system is excellent—once you learn its patterns, the gameplay becomes smooth. Each race has a natural inclination toward certain playstyles, and the zodiac sign grants a useful perk, like enhanced magical power. Your chosen class affects how skills—like archery, armor usage, and alchemy—are divided between major skills (powerful from the start, leveling up quickly) and minor ones (slower to improve). As your skills grow, so does your overall level, prompting you to choose which core attributes to boost. All in all, it's a great system.

A definite must-buy for a fan of The Elder Scrolls series. "Ermagerd Skyrim is better Oblivion sucks cus graphics!!!11! You're just an Oblivion fanboy!11!!!". Well no.

I first started playing The Elder Scrolls series a few years back, when Skyrim first came out because of all the hype. Reason why it shows a ridiculously low number of Skyrim playtime hours on my Steam profile would be that I didn't get the Steam version as I didn't have a Steam account then. I finished the entire main storyline, finished all the DLC, 90% of all sidequests and explored almost 80% of the dungeons in Skyrim.

Now, I only got Oblivion after much insistence by a few of my friends. At first, I was very turned off by the bad graphics and  combat system. I compared it a lot with Skyrim, but I tried to look past the graphics. It was then I got really surprised. Funnily enough, after playing Oblivion for awhile, I like it better than Skyrim. I appreciate and get attached to the characters in Oblivion more than the characters in Skyrim. 

Maybe it's because the character development in Skyrim pale in comparison? Or maybe it is because they hardly (almost never) kill off companions in Skyrim. In Oblivion, a lot of the main characters of the side quests [spoiler] even the main quest [/spoiler] get killed off, and you cannot simply ressurect them using console [spoiler] like if you accidentally kill off Lydia in Skyrim. Face it, everyone does that [/spoiler], because their death is crucial in that plot. 

I like the change of pace in Oblivion compared to the rest of the games I have played so far, because you are not the main hero here. You are just a Blade, assisting the next Emperor to take over the throne and stop Mehrunes Dagon. You do not get to do the final blow to the villian, you do not get to be "hero" at the end of the main storyline. Because someone else close to you will do it for you. And trust me, you will get this feeling of emptiness for a very long time after that.

The soundtrack is really beautiful here, although it may make you feel lonely especially when you are exploring the wilderness. The horses actually make a satisfying galloping sound, although they are not as ridiculous in climbing vertical walls.

If one were to compare Skyrim and Oblivion, I would say they are both incomparable. It's like comparing an apple and an orange. They are similar, but you cannot directly compare them both. If you are looking for something different, and something more story-based, and a f*ck ton of plot twists, go for Oblivion. But if you are more of the graphics, modern-day sandbox game which follows a linear plot, go for Skyrim instead. 

Overall, I enjoy this installment, will definitely put in more hours in this game.
